title: Adjust process priorities safely
goal: Observe actual niceness and the limits of an unprivileged learner.
challenge: Compare default and positively niced owned processes, lower an existing process's priority, and demonstrate an attempted priority increase is denied. Verify actual NI after denial, including a nice command that still runs its program. Clean up; no speed benchmark or privileged success is required.

steps.expected: The actual PID is saved; its NI is normally 0.

steps.explanation: Positive niceness means lower scheduling priority under CPU contention.
steps.expected: A second process starts with NI 12 from this shell's default 0.
NI normally shows 0 and 12. Sleeping tasks do not demonstrate a speed difference.

steps.explanation: On this util-linux tool, -n sets an absolute nice value for an existing PID.
steps.expected: The owned task changes from NI 12 to 15, further lowering its scheduling priority.

steps.explanation: Try to increase its priority again. learner has no capability or resource allowance for this.
steps.expected: Permission denied. Being the owner does not permit raising priority in this guest.

steps.explanation: Check state after the denied change rather than assuming rollback/success.
Try to start above the shell's priority. GNU nice warns on denial but still starts this program at the existing nice value.
steps.expected: A permission warning appears; a real owned sleep still starts. Do not rely on the wrapper warning or exit status alone.

steps.explanation: Verify the command really ran and inspect its actual priority.
After checking identities, terminate and reap the three practice children.
steps.expected: No practice sleeps remain. Higher priority does not mean a guaranteed CPU share.

hints: More positive NI means less scheduling preference; a smaller number means more.
Unprivileged priority lowering works here; raising it again is denied.
Inspect ps NI after errors: GNU nice can still execute the requested program.
review: I observed default and explicitly lowered priority.
I changed an existing owned process and verified NI after a denied increase.
I confirmed a denied nice adjustment still launched its command.
I explained the privilege and performance limits and cleaned up.
coverage: Real guest practice; completion is self-reviewed, with no guest assessment or verification score. Partial LPIC-1 103.6 coverage.
